claim: Signal regulatory protein alpha (SIRPα) is preferentially expressed on thymic portal endothelial cells (TPECs).
source: Here, we found that signal regulatory protein alpha (SIRPα) is preferentially expressed on TPECs.
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-Seq data (Figure 1A, B), RT-PCR analysis (Figure 1D), and flow cytometry data (Figure 1E, F) showing higher SIRPα expression on TPECs compared to other thymic EC subsets.

claim: Disruption of CD47-SIRPα signaling in mice resulted in reduced number of thymic early T cell progenitors (ETPs).
source: Disruption of CD47-SIRPα signaling in mice resulted in reduced number of thymic early T cell progenitors (ETPs), impaired thymic HPC homing, and altered early development of thymocytes.
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing reduced ETP frequencies and numbers in Sirpa-/- mice (Figure 2A, B) and Cd47-/- mice (Figure 4C-E).

claim: Disruption of CD47-SIRPα signaling in mice resulted in impaired thymic HPC homing.
source: Disruption of CD47-SIRPα signaling in mice resulted in reduced number of thymic early T cell progenitors (ETPs), impaired thymic HPC homing, and altered early development of thymocytes.
evidence: Short-term homing assays demonstrated significantly reduced thymic settling of progenitor cells in Sirpa-/- mice (Figure 2G, H, I).

claim: Disruption of CD47-SIRPα signaling in mice resulted in altered early development of thymocytes.
source: Disruption of CD47-SIRPα signaling in mice resulted in reduced number of thymic early T cell progenitors (ETPs), impaired thymic HPC homing, and altered early development of thymocytes.
evidence: The manuscript shows reduced DN thymocyte frequencies and numbers in Sirpa-/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C, D, E) and reduced donor-derived thymocytes after adoptive transfer (Figure 2J, K).

claim: Sirpa-deficient ECs demonstrated impaired transendothelial migration (TEM).
source: Mechanistically, Sirpa-deficient ECs and Cd47-deficient bone marrow progenitor cells or T lymphocytes demonstrated impaired transendothelial migration (TEM).
evidence: Transwell assays showed significantly reduced transmigration of Lin- BMCs across Sirpa-/- EC monolayers (Figure 3F).

claim: Cd47-deficient bone marrow progenitor cells demonstrated impaired transendothelial migration (TEM).
source: Mechanistically, Sirpa-deficient ECs and Cd47-deficient bone marrow progenitor cells or T lymphocytes demonstrated impaired transendothelial migration (TEM).
evidence: Transwell assays showed Cd47-/- Lin- BMCs had significantly less TEM through Cd47-/- MS1 cells compared to WT Lin- BMCs (Figure 4F).

claim: Cd47-deficient T lymphocytes demonstrated impaired transendothelial migration (TEM).
source: Mechanistically, Sirpa-deficient ECs and Cd47-deficient bone marrow progenitor cells or T lymphocytes demonstrated impaired transendothelial migration (TEM).
evidence: Transwell assays showed genetic deficiency of CD47 on T lymphocytes resulted in reduced TEM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).

claim: SIRPα intracellular ITIM motif-initiated downstream signaling in ECs is required for TEM in an SHP2-dependent manner.
source: Specifically, SIRPα intracellular ITIM motif-initiated downstream signaling in ECs was found to be required for TEM in an SHP2- and Src-dependent manner.
evidence: The manuscript shows that Sirpa-Y4F (ITIM motif mutant) failed to rescue TEM in Sirpa-/- ECs (Figure 5B), while constitutively active SHP2 significantly rescued TEM (Figure 5C).

claim: SIRPα intracellular ITIM motif-initiated downstream signaling in ECs is required for TEM in a Src-dependent manner.
source: Specifically, SIRPα intracellular ITIM motif-initiated downstream signaling in ECs was found to be required for TEM in an SHP2- and Src-dependent manner.
evidence: The manuscript shows that Sirpa-/- MS1 cells had significantly deficient active Src (Figure 5D, E), and Src inhibitor PP2 significantly inhibited lymphocyte transmigration (Figure 5J).

claim: CD47 signaling from migrating cells is required for VE-cadherin endocytosis in ECs.
source: Furthermore, CD47 signaling from migrating cells and SIRPα intracellular signaling were found to be required for VE-cadherin endocytosis in ECs.
evidence: Real-time imaging showed significantly higher VE-cadherin/CD31 colocalization (indicating less endocytosis) under migrating cells pretreated with CD47-blocking reagent CV1 compared to control (Figure 6F, G).

claim: SIRPα intracellular signaling is required for VE-cadherin endocytosis in ECs.
source: Furthermore, CD47 signaling from migrating cells and SIRPα intracellular signaling were found to be required for VE-cadherin endocytosis in ECs.
evidence: Sirpa-/- MS1 cells showed significantly lower T-cell-induced VE-cadherin endocytosis (Figure 6A, B), and Sirpa-ΔICD MS1 cells showed similar unresponsiveness (Figure 6C, D).

claim: HPCs enter the thymus via unique blood vessels that are surrounded by perivascular spaces (PVS) primarily in the corticomedullary junction (CMJ) of the thymus.
source: It was reported that HPCs enter the thymus via unique blood vessels that are surrounded by perivascular spaces (PVS) (Lind et al., 2001; Mori et al., 2007) primarily in the corticomedullary junction (CMJ) of the thymus.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lind et al., 2001; Mori et al., 2007).

claim: A specialized subset of P-selectin+Ly6C- thymic portal endothelial cells (TPECs) is located in the CMJ region and associated with PVS structure.
source: Previously, we identified a specialized subset of P-selectin+Ly6C- thymic portal endothelial cells (TPECs) located in the CMJ region and associated with PVS structure, providing the cellular basis for thymic homing of HPCs (Shi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors (Shi et al., 2016).

claim: TPECs are highly associated with settling HPCs.
source: Short-term HPC thymic homing assay confirmed that TPECs is highly associated with settling HPCs and lack of TPECs in lymphotoxin beta receptor-deficient mice resulted in dramatically impaired HPC thymic homing and reduced number of thymic early T cell progenitors (ETPs).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Shi et al., 2016) describing short-term HPC thymic homing assays.

claim: Lack of TPECs in lymphotoxin beta receptor-deficient mice resulted in dramatically impaired HPC thymic homing.
source: Short-term HPC thymic homing assay confirmed that TPECs is highly associated with settling HPCs and lack of TPECs in lymphotoxin beta receptor-deficient mice resulted in dramatically impaired HPC thymic homing and reduced number of thymic early T cell progenitors (ETPs).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Shi et al., 2016).

claim: Lack of TPECs in lymphotoxin beta receptor-deficient mice resulted in reduced number of thymic early T cell progenitors (ETPs).
source: Short-term HPC thymic homing assay confirmed that TPECs is highly associated with settling HPCs and lack of TPECs in lymphotoxin beta receptor-deficient mice resulted in dramatically impaired HPC thymic homing and reduced number of thymic early T cell progenitors (ETPs).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Shi et al., 2016).

claim: TPECs are enriched with transcripts related to cell adhesion and trafficking.
source: Transcriptome analysis revealed that TPECs are enriched with transcripts related to cell adhesion and trafficking, supporting its critical role for thymic homing.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Shi et al., 2016) and by RNA-Seq data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1A).

claim: P-selectin and adhesion molecule VCAM-1 and ICAM-1, highly expressed on ECs, have been suggested to mediate adhesion of HPCs on ECs.
source: P-selectin and adhesion molecule VCAM-1 and ICAM-1, highly expressed on ECs, as also confirmed in our previous study, have been suggested to mediate adhesion of HPCs on ECs (Lind et al., 2001; Mori et al., 2007; Rossi et al., 2005; Scimone et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lind et al., 2001; Mori et al., 2007; Rossi et al., 2005; Scimone et al., 2006).

claim: Chemokines such as CCL25 and CCL19/CCL21 expressed by thymic ECs as well as thymic epithelial cells (TECs) are involved in thymic homing of HPCs, probably via integrin activation.
source: In addition, chemokines such as CCL25 and CCL19/CCL21 expressed by thymic ECs as well as thymic epithelial cells (TECs) are also involved in thymic homing of HPCs, probably via integrin activation (Krueger et al., 2010; Misslitz et al., 2004; Parmo-Cabañas et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2014; Zlotoff et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Krueger et al., 2010; Misslitz et al., 2004; Parmo-Cabañas et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2014; Zlotoff et al., 2010).

claim: Transendothelial migration (TEM) is the decisive step for migration of progenitors from blood into the thymus.
source: Transendothelial migration (TEM) is the decisive step for migration of progenitors from blood into the thymus (Zlotoff and Bhandoola, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Zlotoff and Bhandoola, 2011).

claim: SIRPα is a transmembrane protein that contains three Ig-like domains, a single transmembrane region, and a cytoplasmic region.
source: Signal regulatory protein alpha (SIRPα) is a transmembrane protein that contains three Ig-like domains, a single transmembrane region, and a cytoplasmic region.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of SIRPα.

claim: Ligation of SIRPα by its ligand CD47 transmits intracellular signal through its ITIM motifs.
source: Ligation of SIRPα by its ligand CD47 transmits intracellular signal through its ITIM motifs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SIRPα signaling mechanism.

claim: SIRPα is mainly expressed by myeloid cells such as monocytes, granulocytes, most tissue macrophages, and subsets of dendritic cells.
source: SIRPα is mainly expressed by myeloid cells such as monocytes, granulocytes, most tissue macrophages, and subsets of dendritic cells (Barclay and Van den Berg, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Barclay and Van den Berg, 2014).

claim: CD47 is ubiquitously expressed but shows fluctuating expression levels on different cell states or cell types.
source: On the other hand, CD47 is ubiquitously expressed but show fluctuating expression levels on different cell states or cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD47 expression patterns.

claim: Elevated CD47 expression is detected on bone marrow cells and some of lymphoid subsets.
source: Elevated CD47 expression is detected on bone marrow cells and some of lymphoid subsets (Jaiswal et al., 2009; Van et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Jaiswal et al., 2009; Van et al., 2012).

claim: SIRPα on conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) maintains their survival and proper function via intracellular SHP2 signaling.
source: SIRPα on conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) maintains their survival and proper function via intracellular SHP2 signaling (Iwamura et al., 2011; Saito et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Iwamura et al., 2011; Saito et al., 2010).

claim: On macrophages, upon CD47 ligation, SIRPα signaling activates intracellular SHP1 to inhibit Fcγ receptor-mediated phagocytosis toward target cells.
source: On macrophages, upon CD47 ligation, SIRPα signaling activates intracellular SHP1 to inhibit Fcγ receptor-mediated phagocytosis toward target cells (Blazar et al., 2001; Ishikawa-Sekigami et al., 2006; Tsai and Discher, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Blazar et al., 2001; Ishikawa-Sekigami et al., 2006; Tsai and Discher, 2008).

claim: Elevated expression of CD47 on platelets, lymphocyte subsets, and hematopoietic cell subsets shows 'self' identity and protects them from being cleared by macrophages.
source: Elevated expression of CD47 on platelets, lymphocyte subsets, and hematopoietic cell subsets shows 'self' identity and protects them from being cleared by macrophages (Blazar et al., 2001; Jaiswal et al., 2009; Olsson et al., 2005; Yamao et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Blazar et al., 2001; Jaiswal et al., 2009; Olsson et al., 2005; Yamao et al., 2002).

claim: Tumor cells express high level of CD47 to escape immune surveillance initiated by macrophages.
source: Tumor cells express high level of CD47 to escape immune surveillance initiated by macrophages (Chao et al., 2010; Majeti et al., 2009; Willingham et al., 2012), which leads to the development of CD47-SIRPα blockade as a promising approach for cancer therapy (Feng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Chao et al., 2010; Majeti et al., 2009; Willingham et al., 2012).

claim: CD47-SIRPα blockade is a promising approach for cancer therapy.
source: Tumor cells express high level of CD47 to escape immune surveillance initiated by macrophages (Chao et al., 2010; Majeti et al., 2009; Willingham et al., 2012), which leads to the development of CD47-SIRPα blockade as a promising approach for cancer therapy (Feng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Feng et al., 2019).

claim: SIRPα expressed on cDCs, neutrophils, melanoma cells, and CHO cells has been reported to promote cell motility through SHP2-dependent activation of Rho GTPase and cytoskeleton reorganization.
source: SIRPα expressed on cDCs, neutrophils, melanoma cells, and CHO cells has been reported to promote cell motility (Fukunaga et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2002; Motegi et al., 2003) through SHP2-dependent activation of Rho GTPase (Wollenberg et al., 1996) and cytoskeleton reorganization (Inagaki et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Fukunaga et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2002; Motegi et al., 2003; Wollenberg et al., 1996; Inagaki et al., 2000).

claim: SIRPα expressed on neutrophils and monocytes has been shown to be the ligand for endothelial or epithelial CD47 and promotes junction opening through activating Rho family GTPase therefore permitting transmigration of the SIRPα-expressing cells.
source: On the other hand, SIRPα expressed on neutrophils and monocytes has been shown to be the ligand for endothelial or epithelial CD47 and promotes junction opening through activating Rho family GTPase therefore permitting transmigration of the SIRPα-expressing cells (de Vries et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2002; Stefanidakis et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (de Vries et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2002; Stefanidakis et al., 2008).

claim: SIRPα is among the top 20 signature genes of TPECs that have absolute fold change > 2 and p < 0.01 in TPECs versus either Ly6C+Selp- or Ly6C+Selp+ thymic EC subsets and are in GO term GO_0016477 (cell migration).
source: Expression profile of top 20 signature genes of Ly6C-Selp+ ECs (TPECs), which have absolute FC > 2 and p < 0.01 in TPECs versus either Ly6C+Selp- or Ly6C+Selp+ thymic EC subsets and are in GO term GO_0016477 (cell migration).
evidence: Figure 1A shows a heatmap with SIRPα (Sirpa) among the top 20 signature genes of TPECs based on RNA-Seq data.

claim: SIRPα mRNA expression is highest in TPECs (Ly6C-Selp+) compared to other thymic EC subsets.
source: Real-time PCR analysis of Sirpa mRNA expression in thymic EC subsets, n = 3, each dot represents sample from individual mouse, data are representative of two independent experiments.
evidence: Figure 1D shows quantitative RT-PCR data demonstrating highest Sirpa mRNA expression in TPECs.

claim: SIRPα protein expression is highest on TPECs compared to other thymic EC subsets as measured by mean fluorescence intensity.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of SIRPα expression on the three thymic EC subsets (E) and quantification of measuring mean fluorescence intensity of SIRPα (F), data are representative of three independent experiments with three biological replicates (n=3) in each group.
evidence: Figure 1E and F show flow cytometry data demonstrating highest SIRPα protein expression on TPECs.

claim: SIRPα expression on TPECs is irrespective of the presence of perivascular space (PVS).
source: Immunofluorescence staining also confirmed the location of SIRPα expression on TPECs, although irrespective of PVS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B shows immunofluorescence imaging and statistical analysis indicating similar SIRPα intensity on TPECs with or without PVS.

claim: The remaining TPECs in Ltbr-/- mice showed similar level of SIRPα expression compared to that in WT mice.
source: However, the remaining TPECs in Ltbr-/- mice showed similar level of SIRPα expression compared to that in WT mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1C shows flow cytometry data comparing SIRPα expression on TPECs in WT and Ltbr-/- mice.

claim: Irradiation-induced thymic injury does not alter SIRPα expression on TPECs.
source: Increased thymic stromal niche was found during irradiation (Zlotoff et al., 2011). However, this does not seem to alter SIRPα expression, either (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1D shows flow cytometry data indicating no change in SIRPα expression on TPECs after irradiation.

claim: Sirpa-/- mice appeared grossly normal in thymic development of T cells.
source: Sirpa-/- mice appeared grossly normal in thymic development of T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A shows thymic cellularity data in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: The frequencies and numbers of DN thymocytes were slightly reduced in Sirpa-/- mice.
source: However, the frequencies and numbers of DN thymocytes were slightly reduced (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C shows flow cytometry data demonstrating reduced DN thymocyte proportions and numbers in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: The frequencies and numbers of DN1, DN2, and DN3 thymocytes all exhibited significant reduction in Sirpa-/- mice.
source: More specifically, the frequencies and numbers of DN1, DN2, and DN3 thymocytes all exhibited significant reduction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E shows flow cytometry data demonstrating reduced DN1, DN2, and DN3 thymocyte proportions and numbers in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: Bone marrow multipotent progenitors including lineage-Sca-1+c-Kithigh (LSK) and common lymphoid progenitors (CLPs) remained unchanged in Sirpa-/- mice.
source: Bone marrow multipotent progenitors including lineage-Sca-1+c-Kithigh (LSK) and common lymphoid progenitors (CLPs) remained unchanged in these mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G), suggesting the reduced population size of thymic ETP is unlikely due to impaired generation/homeostasis of bone marrow progenitors.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G shows flow cytometry data indicating no change in LSK and CLP populations in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: Significant decrease of thymic ETP population was found in Sirpa TEK-CKO mice in a degree similar to that in Sirpa-/- mice.
source: Significant decrease of thymic ETP population was found in Sirpa TEK-CKO mice in a degree similar to that in Sirpa-/- mice (Figure 2C and D), suggesting the role of SIRPα is probably mainly derived from ECs.
evidence: Figure 2C and D shows flow cytometry data demonstrating reduced ETP population in Sirpa TEK-CKO mice.

claim: Much lower expression level of SIRPα was found on either medullary or cortical TECs compared to TPECs.
source: In supporting this, much lower expression level of SIRPα was found on either medullary or cortical TECs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C shows flow cytometry data comparing SIRPα expression on TPECs, mTECs, and cTECs.

claim: Mice lacking SIRPα on radioresistant stromal cells demonstrated significantly reduced ETP population.
source: Mice lacking SIRPα on radioresistant stromal cells demonstrated significantly reduced ETP population (Figure 2E and F), whereas in mice lacking SIRPα on hematopoietic cells, ETP population remained unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F).
evidence: Figure 2E and F shows flow cytometry data from bone marrow chimeric mice demonstrating reduced ETP population when SIRPα is absent on radioresistant cells.

claim: In mice lacking SIRPα on hematopoietic cells, ETP population remained unchanged.
source: Mice lacking SIRPα on radioresistant stromal cells demonstrated significantly reduced ETP population (Figure 2E and F), whereas in mice lacking SIRPα on hematopoietic cells, ETP population remained unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F shows flow cytometry data from bone marrow chimeric mice demonstrating unchanged ETP population when SIRPα is absent on hematopoietic cells.

claim: SIRPα deficiency on hematopoietic cells did not result in impaired thymic settling of bone marrow progenitors.
source: SIRPα deficiency on hematopoietic cells did not result in impaired thymic settling of bone marrow progenitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G), nor did the number of progenitors retained in the periphery as represented by the number of progenitor cells in the spleen (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2G shows short-term homing assay data in bone marrow chimeric mice.

claim: Loss of SIRPα on radioresistant cells significantly impeded thymic entry of progenitor cells.
source: On the contrary, loss of SIRPα on radioresistant cells significantly impeded thymic entry of progenitor cells (Figure 2G and H), while the number of donor bone marrow cells retained unaltered in the periphery (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: Figure 2G and H shows short-term homing assay data demonstrating reduced thymic settling of progenitors in mice lacking SIRPα on radioresistant cells.

claim: Short-term homing of Lin- BMCs showed significant defect in Sirpa-/- mice in a more physiologically relevant setting.
source: In this more physiologically relevant setting, short-term homing of Lin- BMCs still showed significant defect in Sirpa-/- mice (Figure 2I).
evidence: Figure 2I shows short-term homing assay data using enriched Lin- BMCs in non-irradiated mice.

claim: Donor-derived cells have developed through all major stages of thymocytes 3 weeks after adoptive transfer of Lin- BMCs.
source: To test whether the defective thymic homing of progenitor cells in Sirpa-/- mice would influence T cell development, we examined donor-derived thymocytes 3 weeks after adoptive transfer. At this time point, donor-derived cells have developed through all major stages of thymocytes (Figure 2J), and significantly less repopulated in Sirpa-/- mice, especially for DP thymocytes (Figure 2J).
evidence: Figure 2J shows flow cytometry data of donor-derived thymocyte subsets 3 weeks after adoptive transfer.

claim: Donor-derived cells significantly less repopulated in Sirpa-/- mice 3 weeks after adoptive transfer, especially for DP thymocytes.
source: At this time point, donor-derived cells have developed through all major stages of thymocytes (Figure 2J), and significantly less repopulated in Sirpa-/- mice, especially for DP thymocytes (Figure 2J).
evidence: Figure 2J shows flow cytometry data demonstrating reduced donor-derived thymocyte subsets in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: The total thymocytes derived from donor progenitor cells is reduced in Sirpa-/- mice 3 weeks after adoptive transfer.
source: The total thymocytes derived from donor progenitor cells is also reduced in Sirpa-/- mice (Figure 2K).
evidence: Figure 2K shows flow cytometry data demonstrating reduced total donor-derived thymocytes in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: Sirpa-/- mice did not show altered thymic endothelial development in regard to the percentage and number of total ECs.
source: Since TPECs is the portal of thymic progenitor entry, we asked whether SIRPα signaling may regulate TPEC development. Sirpa-/- mice did not show altered thymic endothelial development in regard to the percentage and number of total ECs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C) and specifically TPECs (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C shows flow cytometry data indicating no change in total EC percentage and number in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: Sirpa-/- mice did not show altered thymic endothelial development in regard to the percentage and number of TPECs.
source: Sirpa-/- mice did not show altered thymic endothelial development in regard to the percentage and number of total ECs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C) and specifically TPECs (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Figure 3A-C shows flow cytometry data indicating no change in TPEC percentage and number in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: P-selectin expression on TPECs showed no significant change in Sirpa TEK-CKO mice.
source: P-selectin, VCAM-1, Ccl25, and Ccl19 showed no significant change on TPECs of Sirpa-/- mice (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 3D shows flow cytometry data indicating no change in P-selectin expression on TPECs in Sirpa TEK-CKO mice.

claim: VCAM-1 expression on TPECs showed no significant change in Sirpa-/- mice.
source: P-selectin, VCAM-1, Ccl25, and Ccl19 showed no significant change on TPECs of Sirpa-/- mice (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 3E shows flow cytometry data indicating no change in VCAM-1 expression on TPECs in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: Ccl25 expression on TPECs showed no significant change in Sirpa-/- mice.
source: P-selectin, VCAM-1, Ccl25, and Ccl19 showed no significant change on TPECs of Sirpa-/- mice (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1D shows RT-PCR data indicating no change in Ccl25 expression on TPECs in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: Ccl19 expression on TPECs showed no significant change in Sirpa-/- mice.
source: P-selectin, VCAM-1, Ccl25, and Ccl19 showed no significant change on TPECs of Sirpa-/- mice (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1D shows RT-PCR data indicating no change in Ccl19 expression on TPECs in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: Ccl21a showed slight but significantly reduced expression in Sirpa-/- EC.
source: Only Ccl21a showed slight but significantly reduced expression in Sirpa-/- EC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1D shows RT-PCR data indicating reduced Ccl21a expression in Sirpa-/- ECs.

claim: Compared to WT ECs, Sirpa-/- EC monolayer mediates comparable adhesion of lymphocytes.
source: Compared to WT ECs, Sirpa-/- EC monolayer mediates comparable adhesion of lymphocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1F shows in vitro adhesion assay data indicating no difference in lymphocyte adhesion between WT and Sirpa-/- ECs.

claim: Monolayers of both WT and Sirpa-/- ECs were equally formed at the time of transmigration assay.
source: Next, we examined the role of SIRPα in TEM by transwell assay. Monolayers of both WT and Sirpa-/- ECs were equally formed at the time of transmigration assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H shows flow cytometry and microscopy data indicating similar EC monolayer formation.

claim: A similar effect of reduced TEM was found when naïve T lymphocytes were used for transwell assay.
source: A similar effect was also found when naïve T lymphocytes were used for transwell assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), suggesting a general mechanism of endothelial SIRPα in controlling TEM.
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1I shows transwell assay data demonstrating reduced lymphocyte TEM across Sirpa-/- ECs.

claim: Among developmental subsets of T cell lineage, ETPs exhibited the highest level of CD47 expression.
source: Interestingly, we found among developmental subsets of T cell lineage, ETPs exhibited the highest level of CD47 expression (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting preferential interaction may exist between ETPs and TPECs controlling thymic progenitor homing and ETP population.
evidence: Figure 4A shows flow cytometry data demonstrating highest CD47 expression on ETPs among T cell lineage subsets.

claim: FACS staining revealed higher level of CD47 expression on the more primitive Flt3hi ETP subset.
source: Moreover, FACS staining revealed higher level of CD47 expression on the more primitive Flt3hi ETP subset (Figure 4B, gating strategy: Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows flow cytometry data demonstrating higher CD47 expression on Flt3hi ETPs compared to Flt3lo ETPs.

claim: Cd47-/- mice showed significantly reduced ETP population.
source: Indeed, Cd47-/- mice showed significantly reduced ETP population (Figure 4C–E) and unaffected ancestral progenitor subsets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E), similar to that of Sirpa-/- mice.
evidence: Figure 4C-E shows flow cytometry data demonstrating reduced ETP population in Cd47-/- mice.

claim: Cd47-/- mice showed unaffected ancestral progenitor subsets.
source: Indeed, Cd47-/- mice showed significantly reduced ETP population (Figure 4C–E) and unaffected ancestral progenitor subsets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E), similar to that of Sirpa-/- mice.
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E shows flow cytometry data indicating no change in LSK populations in Cd47-/- mice.

claim: Significantly elevated CD47 expression was found on immortalized MS1 cells.
source: It should be noted that significantly elevated CD47 expression was found on immortalized cells, herein MS1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), which was not found in the physiological situation, wherein TPEC-CD47 expression level is much lower than that on migrating cells (ETP) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1F shows flow cytometry data demonstrating elevated CD47 expression on MS1 cells compared to primary lymphocytes.

claim: TPEC-CD47 expression level is much lower than that on migrating cells (ETP) in the physiological situation.
source: It should be noted that significantly elevated CD47 expression was found on immortalized cells, herein MS1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), which was not found in the physiological situation, wherein TPEC-CD47 expression level is much lower than that on migrating cells (ETP) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, H shows flow cytometry data comparing CD47 expression on TPECs and ETPs.

claim: Lymphocyte transmigration across Cd47-/- MS1 was significantly reduced compared to that on WT MS1.
source: Thus, although lymphocyte transmigration across Cd47-/- MS1 was significantly reduced compared to that on WT MS1, it probably does not reflect a physiological role (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I, J).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1I, J shows transwell assay data demonstrating reduced lymphocyte TEM across Cd47-/- MS1 cells.

claim: Genetic deficiency of CD47 on T lymphocytes showed reduced TEM.
source: Similarly, genetic deficiency of CD47 or blockade of CD47 signal on T lymphocytes also showed reduced TEM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, L).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1K shows transwell assay data demonstrating reduced TEM of Cd47-/- T lymphocytes.

claim: Blockade of CD47 signal on T lymphocytes showed reduced TEM.
source: Similarly, genetic deficiency of CD47 or blockade of CD47 signal on T lymphocytes also showed reduced TEM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, L).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1L shows transwell assay data demonstrating reduced TEM of CV1-treated lymphocytes.

claim: T lymphocyte transmigration across Sirpa-ΔICD MS1 cells reduced to the level similar to that on Sirpa-/- MS1 cells.
source: However, T lymphocyte transmigration across Sirpa-ΔICD MS1 cells reduced to the level similar to that on Sirpa-/- MS1 cells (Figure 5A), suggesting SIRPα regulates TEM mainly through ECs.
evidence: Figure 5A shows transwell assay data demonstrating reduced lymphocyte TEM across Sirpa-ΔICD MS1 cells.

claim: Lentiviral transduction with WT Sirpa coding sequence (Sirpa-WT) in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells largely recovered TEM.
source: Furthermore, lentiviral transduction with WT Sirpa coding sequence (Sirpa-WT) in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells largely recovered TEM (Figure 5B), whereas transduction with loss-of-function mutant Sirpa-Y4F, in which all four functional tyrosine residues in the cytoplasmic ITIM motifs were substituted with inactive phenylalanine, failed in TEM rescue (Figure 5B), even with restored surface expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 5B shows transwell assay data demonstrating TEM recovery in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells transduced with WT Sirpa.

claim: Transduction with loss-of-function mutant Sirpa-Y4F failed in TEM rescue.
source: Furthermore, lentiviral transduction with WT Sirpa coding sequence (Sirpa-WT) in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells largely recovered TEM (Figure 5B), whereas transduction with loss-of-function mutant Sirpa-Y4F, in which all four functional tyrosine residues in the cytoplasmic ITIM motifs were substituted with inactive phenylalanine, failed in TEM rescue (Figure 5B), even with restored surface expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 5B shows transwell assay data demonstrating failure of TEM rescue in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells transduced with Sirpa-Y4F.

claim: Shp2-CA MS1 cells permitted significantly more TEM of T lymphocytes.
source: Shp2-CA MS1 cells permitted significantly more TEM of T lymphocytes (Figure 5C), demonstrating that SHP2 activation can rescue the defective effect of SIRPα deficiency.
evidence: Figure 5C shows transwell assay data demonstrating increased TEM in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells expressing constitutively active SHP2.

claim: In Sirpa-/- MS1 cells, active Src (pTyr-416) was significantly deficient compared to WT.
source: In Sirpa-/- MS1 cells, active Src (pTyr-416) was significantly deficient compared to WT (Figure 5D and E) without affecting the pool of autoinhibitory inactive form of Src (pTyr-529) (Figure 5D and F).
evidence: Figure 5D and E shows Western blot data demonstrating reduced active Src (pY416-Src) in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells.

claim: SIRPα deficiency in MS1 cells does not affect the pool of autoinhibitory inactive form of Src (pTyr-529).
source: In Sirpa-/- MS1 cells, active Src (pTyr-416) was significantly deficient compared to WT (Figure 5D and E) without affecting the pool of autoinhibitory inactive form of Src (pTyr-529) (Figure 5D and F).
evidence: Figure 5D and F shows Western blot data indicating no change in inactive Src (pY529-Src) in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells.

claim: Plate-bound CD47 significantly promoted Src activation (pTyr-416) in Cd47-/- MS1 cells.
source: Furthermore, plate-bound CD47 significantly promoted Src activation (pTyr-416,) but not pTyr-529 in Cd47-/- MS1 cells (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: Figure 5G and H shows Western blot data demonstrating increased active Src (pY416-Src) in Cd47-/- MS1 cells upon CD47 stimulation.

claim: Plate-bound CD47 did not affect pTyr-529 Src in Cd47-/- MS1 cells.
source: Furthermore, plate-bound CD47 significantly promoted Src activation (pTyr-416,) but not pTyr-529 in Cd47-/- MS1 cells (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: Figure 5G and I shows Western blot data indicating no change in inactive Src (pY529-Src) in Cd47-/- MS1 cells upon CD47 stimulation.

claim: Significantly inhibited lymphocyte transmigration was observed upon PP2 treatment of WT MS1 cells.
source: To directly assess the role of Src in leukocyte transmigration, a specific inhibitor of Src family kinases, PP2, was applied to the WT MS1 cells during transwell assay. Significantly inhibited lymphocyte transmigration was observed upon PP2 treatment (Figure 5J).
evidence: Figure 5J shows transwell assay data demonstrating reduced lymphocyte TEM upon PP2 treatment.

claim: The surface expression of VE-cadherin is not altered in Sirpa-/- ECs.
source: The surface expression of VE-cadherin is not altered in Sirpa-/- ECs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B shows confocal microscopy data indicating no change in VE-cadherin surface expression in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells.

claim: Upon T lymphocyte engagement, Sirpa-/- MS1 showed significantly lower T-cell-induced VE-cadherin endocytosis.
source: Upon T lymphocyte engagement, Sirpa-/- MS1 showed significantly lower T-cell-induced VE-cadherin endocytosis (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Figure 6A and B shows confocal microscopy data demonstrating reduced VE-cadherin endocytosis in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells upon lymphocyte engagement.

claim: Sirpa-ΔICD MS1 cells showed similar unresponsiveness of VE-cadherin endocytosis to lymphocyte engagement.
source: Sirpa-ΔICD MS1 cells showed similar unresponsiveness of VE-cadherin endocytosis to lymphocyte engagement (Figure 6C and D), demonstrating the requirement of SIRPα intracellular signaling in facilitating VE-cadherin endocytosis.
evidence: Figure 6C and D shows confocal microscopy data demonstrating reduced VE-cadherin endocytosis in Sirpa-ΔICD MS1 cells upon lymphocyte engagement.

claim: Inhibition of SIRPα downstream molecule Src by PP2 significantly inhibited endocytosis of VE-cadherin in WT MS1 cells but not in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of SIRPα downstream molecule Src by PP2 also significantly inhibited endocytosis of VE-cadherin in WT MS1 cells but not in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells (Figure 6E), suggesting an important role of Src activity downstream of SIRPα intracellular signaling in controlling VE-cadherin endocytosis.
evidence: Figure 6E shows confocal microscopy data demonstrating reduced VE-cadherin endocytosis in WT MS1 cells upon PP2 treatment but not in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells.

claim: Significantly higher degree of VE-cadherin/CD31 colocalization was found under migrating cells that were pretreated with CV-1 compared to that under control treatment.
source: Significantly higher degree of VE-cadherin/CD31 colocalization was found under migrating cells that were pretreated with CV-1 compared to that under control treatment (Figure 6F and G), suggesting the requirement of CD47 signal derived from migrating cells for induction of VE-cadherin endocytosis.
evidence: Figure 6F and G shows real-time imaging data demonstrating higher VE-cadherin/CD31 colocalization under CV1-treated migrating cells.

claim: VE-cadherin is the dominant gate-keeping molecule controlling leukocyte transmigrating through endothelial barrier.
source: VE-cadherin is the dominant gate-keeping molecule controlling leukocyte transmigrating through endothelial barrier (Corada et al., 1999; Vestweber, 2007; Vestweber et al., 2009; Wessel et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Corada et al., 1999; Vestweber, 2007; Vestweber et al., 2009; Wessel et al., 2014).

claim: VE-cadherin controls junction opening by regulated destabilization and endocytosis from junctional area of cell surface.
source: VE-cadherin controls junction opening by regulated destabilization and endocytosis from junctional area of cell surface (Allingham et al., 2007; Benn et al., 2016; Wessel et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Allingham et al., 2007; Benn et al., 2016; Wessel et al., 2014).

claim: Phosphatase SHP2 and kinase Src have been both reported to destabilize adherens junction during transmigration by promoting endocytosis of VE-cadherin.
source: In addition, phosphatase SHP2 and kinase Src have been both reported to destabilize adherens junction during transmigration by promoting endocytosis of VE-cadherin (Allingham et al., 2007; Wessel et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Allingham et al., 2007; Wessel et al., 2014).

claim: SHP2 activation can regulate Src family kinase activity by controlling Csk recruitment.
source: It has been reported that SHP2 activation can regulate Src family kinase activity by controlling Csk recruitment (Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Zhang et al., 2004).

claim: CD47-SIRPα signal activates SHP2-Src axis to control VE-cadherin endocytosis and TEM.
source: Therefore, it is possible that CD47-SIRPα signal activates SHP2-Src axis to control VE-cadherin endocytosis and TEM.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that SIRPα signaling activates both SHP2 and Src, and both are required for VE-cadherin endocytosis and TEM.

claim: At steady state, thymocyte development in Sirpa-/- mice shows slight and significant defect at DN stage compared to that in WT mice.
source: In Sirpa-/- mice, at steady state, thymocyte development shows slight and significant defect at DN stage compared to that in WT mice, while later stage development appears normal.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C shows flow cytometry data demonstrating reduced DN thymocyte proportions and numbers in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: Later stage thymocyte development appears normal in Sirpa-/- mice at steady state.
source: In Sirpa-/- mice, at steady state, thymocyte development shows slight and significant defect at DN stage compared to that in WT mice, while later stage development appears normal.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, C shows flow cytometry data indicating normal DP, CD4 SP, and CD8 SP thymocyte development in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: Upon Lin- BMC adoptive transfer, thymocyte development in Sirpa-/- mice is significantly impaired at both DN and DP stages.
source: In another scenario, upon Lin- BMC adoptive transfer, thymocyte development in Sirpa-/- mice is also significantly impaired at both DN and DP stages.
evidence: Figure 2J shows flow cytometry data demonstrating reduced donor-derived DN and DP thymocytes in Sirpa-/- mice after adoptive transfer.

claim: There is a trend of reduction of CD4+ and CD8+ SP thymocytes in Sirpa-/- mice upon Lin- BMC adoptive transfer, although no statistical significance was achieved.
source: While no statistical significance was achieved, there is a trend of reduction of CD4+ and CD8+ SP thymocytes in Sirpa-/- mice.
evidence: Figure 2J shows flow cytometry data with a trend toward reduced donor-derived CD4 SP and CD8 SP thymocytes in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: Elevated CD47 on migrating progenitors may engage SIRPα on specialized TPECs to promote their thymic entry.
source: Thus, CD47 expression on immune cells is correlated with enhanced transmigration. These data suggest that elevated CD47 on migrating progenitors may engage SIRPα on specialized TPECs to promote their thymic entry.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing highest CD47 expression on ETPs and the requirement of CD47 for TEM.

claim: SIRPα regulates TEM mainly through ECs.
source: However, T lymphocyte transmigration across Sirpa-ΔICD MS1 cells reduced to the level similar to that on Sirpa-/- MS1 cells (Figure 5A), suggesting SIRPα regulates TEM mainly through ECs.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that deletion of SIRPα intracellular domain (which retains extracellular domain for potential reverse signaling) results in TEM defect similar to complete SIRPα deletion.

claim: SHP2 activation can rescue the defective effect of SIRPα deficiency on TEM.
source: Shp2-CA MS1 cells permitted significantly more TEM of T lymphocytes (Figure 5C), demonstrating that SHP2 activation can rescue the defective effect of SIRPα deficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that constitutively active SHP2 expression in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells significantly increases TEM.

claim: SIRPα downstream signaling has the ability to activate Src kinase.
source: These data suggest the ability of SIRPα downstream signaling in activating Src kinase.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing reduced active Src in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells and increased active Src upon CD47 stimulation.

claim: Src kinase is involved in SIRPα signal-induced VE-cadherin endocytosis.
source: Thus, Src kinase is also involved in SIRPα signal-induced VE-cadherin endocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that Src inhibitor PP2 reduces VE-cadherin endocytosis in WT MS1 cells but not in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells.

claim: CD47 signal derived from migrating cells is required for induction of VE-cadherin endocytosis.
source: Significantly higher degree of VE-cadherin/CD31 colocalization was found under migrating cells that were pretreated with CV-1 compared to that under control treatment (Figure 6F and G), suggesting the requirement of CD47 signal derived from migrating cells for induction of VE-cadherin endocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that CD47 blockade on migrating cells results in less VE-cadherin endocytosis (higher VE-cadherin/CD31 colocalization).

claim: Src activity downstream of SIRPα intracellular signaling plays an important role in controlling VE-cadherin endocytosis.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of SIRPα downstream molecule Src by PP2 also significantly inhibited endocytosis of VE-cadherin in WT MS1 cells but not in Sirpa-/- MS1 cells (Figure 6E), suggesting an important role of Src activity downstream of SIRPα intracellular signaling in controlling VE-cadherin endocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that Src inhibitor reduces VE-cadherin endocytosis in WT but not Sirpa-/- MS1 cells.

claim: The reduced population size of thymic ETP in Sirpa-/- mice is unlikely due to impaired generation/homeostasis of bone marrow progenitors.
source: Bone marrow multipotent progenitors including lineage-Sca-1+c-Kithigh (LSK) and common lymphoid progenitors (CLPs) remained unchanged in these mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G), suggesting the reduced population size of thymic ETP is unlikely due to impaired generation/homeostasis of bone marrow progenitors.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing normal LSK and CLP populations in Sirpa-/- mice.

claim: The role of SIRPα is probably mainly derived from ECs.
source: Significant decrease of thymic ETP population was found in Sirpa TEK-CKO mice in a degree similar to that in Sirpa-/- mice (Figure 2C and D), suggesting the role of SIRPα is probably mainly derived from ECs.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing similar ETP reduction in Sirpa TEK-CKO mice (which deletes SIRPα in ECs and hematopoietic cells) and Sirpa-/- mice, combined with low SIRPα expression on TECs.

claim: Reduced thymic ETP population in Sirpa-/- or Sirpa TEK-CKO mice is unlikely due to increased clearance of HPCs in the absence of hematopoietic SIRPα.
source: Thus, together with the previous data, reduced thymic ETP population in Sirpa-/- or Sirpa TEK-CKO mice is unlikely due to increased clearance of HPCs in the absence of hematopoietic SIRPα.
evidence: This is inferred from the bone marrow chimera data showing that SIRPα deficiency on hematopoietic cells does not affect ETP population.

claim: The reduced Ccl21a expression in Sirpa-/- EC unlikely explains the significant ETP reduction in Sirpa-/- mice.
source: Considering unreduced thymic ETP population in CCR7-deficient mice, the reduced Ccl21a expression in Sirpa-/- EC unlikely explains the significant ETP reduction in Sirpa-/- mice.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge about CCR7-deficient mice and the observation of reduced Ccl21a expression in Sirpa-/- ECs.

claim: Endothelial SIRPα plays a direct role in controlling progenitor cell TEM.
source: Remarkably, SIRPα deficiency in ECs resulted in significant reduction of transmigrated cell numbers (Figure 3F), suggesting a direct role of endothelial SIRPα in controlling progenitor cell TEM.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro transwell assay data showing reduced TEM across Sirpa-/- EC monolayers.

claim: Endothelial SIRPα plays a general role in controlling TEM.
source: A similar effect was also found when naïve T lymphocytes were used for transwell assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), suggesting a general mechanism of endothelial SIRPα in controlling TEM.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing reduced TEM of both Lin- BMCs and T lymphocytes across Sirpa-/- ECs.

claim: Preferential interaction may exist between ETPs and TPECs controlling thymic progenitor homing and ETP population.
source: Interestingly, we found among developmental subsets of T cell lineage, ETPs exhibited the highest level of CD47 expression (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting preferential interaction may exist between ETPs and TPECs controlling thymic progenitor homing and ETP population.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing highest CD47 expression on ETPs and preferential SIRPα expression on TPECs.

claim: Lymphocyte transmigration across Cd47-/- MS1 probably does not reflect a physiological role of endothelial CD47.
source: Thus, although lymphocyte transmigration across Cd47-/- MS1 was significantly reduced compared to that on WT MS1, it probably does not reflect a physiological role (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I, J).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of artificial hyperexpression of CD47 on MS1 cells compared to physiological TPEC CD47 expression.

claim: CD47 expression on immune cells is correlated with enhanced transmigration.
source: Thus, CD47 expression on immune cells is correlated with enhanced transmigration.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing reduced TEM of Cd47-/- Lin- BMCs and lymphocytes, and blockade of CD47 on lymphocytes.

claim: SIRPα intracellular ITIMs-mediated downstream signaling in ECs is required for TEM.
source: Thus, SIRPα intracellular ITIMs-mediated downstream signaling in ECs is required for TEM.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that Sirpa-Y4F (ITIM mutant) fails to rescue TEM and Sirpa-ΔICD shows TEM defect.

claim: SIRPα signal-induced VE-cadherin endocytosis is at least in part through ITIM-SHP2 pathway.
source: Together with the fact that ITIM motif activates cytosolic SHP2 phosphatase (Motegi et al., 2003; Tsuda et al., 1998), these data suggest that SIRPα signal-induced VE-cadherin endocytosis is at least in part through ITIM-SHP2 pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that ITIM mutant fails to rescue TEM, constitutively active SHP2 rescues TEM, and established knowledge about ITIM-SHP2 signaling.

claim: ITIM motif activates cytosolic SHP2 phosphatase.
source: Together with the fact that ITIM motif activates cytosolic SHP2 phosphatase (Motegi et al., 2003; Tsuda et al., 1998), these data suggest that SIRPα signal-induced VE-cadherin endocytosis is at least in part through ITIM-SHP2 pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Motegi et al., 2003; Tsuda et al., 1998).

claim: The requirement of SIRPα intracellular signaling in facilitating VE-cadherin endocytosis is demonstrated.
source: Sirpa-ΔICD MS1 cells showed similar unresponsiveness of VE-cadherin endocytosis to lymphocyte engagement (Figure 6C and D), demonstrating the requirement of SIRPα intracellular signaling in facilitating VE-cadherin endocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that Sirpa-ΔICD MS1 cells have reduced VE-cadherin endocytosis similar to Sirpa-/- MS1 cells.

claim: CD47-SIRPα signal regulates VE-cadherin endocytosis via activation of SHP2 and Src kinase, at sites of contact, to control TEM.
source: These data suggest that upon migrating cell contacts, CD47-SIRPα signal regulates VE-cadherin endocytosis via activation of SHP2 and Src kinase, at sites of contact, to control TEM.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing CD47 and SIRPα requirements, SHP2 and Src involvement, and VE-cadherin endocytosis regulation.
